citeinfo.title: Tree ring dataset for a regional avalanche chronology in Colorado 1319-2022

descript.abstract: This dataset includes processed tree ring data from avalanche paths throughout Colorado, USA. The data were processed in three distinct phases that resulted in this dataset: collection, processing, and avalanche signal analysis. This dataset consists of samples from 1188 cross-sections and increment cores from 1023 individual trees within 24 avalanche paths across the region. From these samples 4135 probable avalanche related growth disturbances were identified.
descript.purpose: These data were collected as part of the USGS Snow and Avalanche Project of the U.S. Geological Survey Ecosystems Mission Area Climate Research and Development Program. Understanding avalanche processes and associated large magnitude avalanche return intervals is critical for local and regional avalanche forecasting operations, transportation agencies, and planners. These data can be used to examine large magnitude avalanche patterns on both temporal and spatial scales. This dataset ultimately serves to enhance public and worker safety, and understand landscape disturbance processes and change in mountain ecosystems.

attracc.attraccr:
The sampled tree-rings were dated to the exact calendar year of formation using the traditional pattern matching method of skeleton plot cross-dating (Stokes and Smiley 1995). The annual growth rings were then measured to 0.001 millimeter (mm) precision and the measurements were submitted to the quality control dating program COFECHA (Holmes 1983) for statistical verification. The accuracy of the tree-ring dating is verified through statistical tests that express the positive association between the measured time series and positively dated reference regional tree-ring chronology time series that have been subjected to peer-review and available on the International Tree-Ring Databank (ITRDB website). Most measured series exhibited the interseries correlation coefficient or Pearson coefficient (i.e. r-value) widely accepted as significant (p-value < 0.05) and verifiably dated. R-value correlations for each sample and each site master chronology exceeded the 99% confidence level of r = 0.3281 for the 50 year segment length (Grissino-Mayer 2001). The dated tree-ring measurement series were then combined to compute a master dating series for each site. A list of marker growth years was recorded from the master series, i.e. years when multiple trees experienced exceptionally stressed or narrow growth and years of exceptionally wide or productive growth. Some samples were too young to pass the COFECHA program r-value test (i.e. samples containing less than 50 rings). Therefore, the master series in the form of skeleton plots and marker year lists was used to visually cross-date those samples that did not contain a sufficient amount of tree-rings. The young and complacent samples unable to pass statistical tests were also confidently dated using observed mortality events (i.e. the outermost ring is known because the tree was killed in an observed avalanche event). In some cases samples may contain distinct early wood growth on the outermost ring, which is commonly observed in trees killed in the early growing season by spring avalanches. This visual dating method for young or very complacent tree-ring series can be replicated and verified through expert analysis by trained dendrochronologists. The samples that were not successfully dated using statistical verification or confident visual dating were omitted from the study, therefore the dated tree-rings and the calendar dates assigned to the traumatic event signals presented in the dataset are considered “true” values.
Grissino-Mayer, H.D. 2001. Evaluating crossdating accuracy: a manual and tutorial for the computer program COFECHA. Tree-Ring Research. 57. Holmes, R.L. 1983. Computer-assisted quality control in tree-ring dating and measurement. Tree Ring Bulletin 44: 69–78. Stokes, M.A., and T.L. Smiley. 1995. An introduction to tree-ring dating. Tucson: University Arizona Press.

dataqual.logic: The data match with the details provided in the methods as based on previous literature. The data have been checked for duplicates and omissions.
dataqual.complete: The dataset represents avalanche reconstructions from these specific avalanche paths only. Our study site consists of 24 avalanche paths throughout Colorado, USA. We collected 13 to 68 samples in each of the 24 avalanche paths in six Colorado counties and three major sub-regions (North, Central, and South). The avalanche paths in each sub-region encompass a range of spatial extents from adjacent to ~68 km apart. The largest distance between any two sub-regions (North to South) is ~245 km. The sites are adjacent to roads, ski areas, neighborhoods, utilities infrastructure, power transmission lines, and recreational access points. The cross sections were collected from dead (both downed and standing dead) trees, and the cores were collected from live trees. We emphasized the selection of quality trees and consideration of location, size, and potential age of tree samples. A limitation of all dendrochronology studies in avalanche paths is that large magnitude events cause extensive damage and high tree mortality, thereby reducing subsequent potential tree-ring records. We utilized cross-sections, a large sample size, and a unique spatial sampling strategy in this study for a more robust analysis as signals can be lost or misidentified in cores.

procstep.procdesc: Cross-sectional wood samples were taken at the location of an external scar or just above the root buttress from downed and dead tree stems, standing dead trees and from stumps of trees that suffered topping from avalanche-damage. Tree-ring core samples were taken non-destructively from live trees using a 5mm diameter increment borer. Core samples were extracted from live trees with obvious scaring or flagging along the avalanche path margins and run-out zone. Metadata including photographs, GPS coordinates and notes regarding the amount of scarring, relative location of the tree in the path and upslope direction were recorded along with other field notes . The characteristics that identified the tree to be in-place vs. transported from it’s original growth position were recorded (i.e. presence or absence of roots attached to the ground or the distance from an obvious excavated area where the tree was uprooted). The sampling strategy targeted an even number of samples collected from both margins at varying elevations, trees located anywhere in the main path and trees in the run out zone.

Cross-sections were dried and stabilized to prevent radial cracking and further rot. Samples were sanded to a fine polish to expose the anatomy of each growth ring. Cores and cross-sections were cross-dated with each other using the skeleton plot method to account for missing and false-rings (Stokes and Smiley 1995). A site composite chronology was developed using live-tree core samples and dead tree cross-sections. The site composite was successfully cross-dated with preexisting regional chronologies to confirm the exact calendar dating of each tree-ring (International Tree-Ring Database). The widths of the dated tree-rings were measured to 0.001mm precision using a sliding stage micrometer. The ring-width measurements for each sample were submitted to the dating quality control COFECHA for statistical verification (Holmes 1983).
Holmes, R.L. 1983. Computer-assisted quality control in tree-ring dating and measurement. Tree Ring Bulletin 44: 69–78. Stokes, M.A., and Smiley, T.L. 1995. An introduction to tree-ring dating. Tucson: University Arizona Press.

The dated cross-sections were analyzed for signs of traumatic impact events that could be associated to snow avalanche activity. A system of classification ratings ranked 1 through 5 was designed and adapted from previous dendrogeomorphological studies to qualify the severity of the trauma and tree growth response (Reardon et al 2008). A range of anatomical markers were recorded. The 1 through 5 debris impact trauma classification ratings are defined as follows: Class 1 (C-1) Clear impact scar associated with well-defined reaction wood, growth suppression or major traumatic resin duct development. And/or the strong presence of some combination of these major anatomical markers of trauma and growth response recorded in multiple years of growth and occurring at a year that multiple samples at the site record similar trauma and scaring. C-1 events are also assigned to the death date of trees killed by observed avalanche mortality at the collection site; the presence of earlywood indicates an early season avalanche killed the tree. Class 2 (C-2) Scar or small scar recorded in the first ten years of tree growth without associated reaction wood, growth suppression or traumatic resin ducts. Or, obvious reaction wood, growth suppression or significant presence of traumatic resin ducts that occurs abruptly after normal growth that lasts for 3 or more years. Class 3 (C-3) The presence of reaction wood, growth suppression or traumatic resin ducts recorded in less than 3 successive growth years. Class 4 (C-4) Poorly defined reaction wood, growth suppression or minimal presence of traumatic resin ducts lasting 1-2 years or a C-3 class event occurring in the first 10 years of tree growth where the cause of damage could result from various biological and environmental conditions. Class 5 (C-5) Very poorly defined reaction wood, growth suppression or minimal presence of traumatic resin ducts isolated in one growth year or a C-4 class event occurring in the first 10 years of tree growth where the cause of damage could result from various biological and environmental conditions. Class 6 (C-6) Frist rings with associated cellular disruption in earlywood. This rating was included in the tree-ring analysis, but not included in the avalanche signal analysis. We include it here for completeness of the dataset and any future analysis.
Reardon, B.A. Pederson, G.T., Caruso, C.J., and Fagre, D.B. 2008. Spatial Reconstructions and Comparisons of Historic Snow Avalanche Frequency and Extent Using Tree Rings in Glacier National Park, Montana, U.S.A. Arctic, Antarctic, and Alpine Research, 40:1 148-160
